lead.headline: Tandy 1000 brings PC compatibility home
lead.dek: Radio Shack’s November newcomer combines an 8088 with colorful graphics, three-voice sound and bundled DeskMate.
body: Radio Shack has a new contender for the home-computer desk this November. The Tandy 1000 puts an Intel 8088 inside a machine intended to offer compatibility with most IBM PC software, while retaining the enhanced graphics and sound associated with the PCjr. It is a practical pitch to households that want work and play in the same cabinet.

The original configuration carries 128 KB of memory, expandable to 640 KB. Sixteen-color PCjr-compatible graphics, three-voice sound and joystick ports make the entertainment side more than an afterthought. For buyers comparing machines by their game screens as well as their word processors, those features deserve a place beside the processor specification.

DeskMate comes bundled with the machine, giving the buyer a software starting point. Radio Shack stores and Computer Centers provide the retail route. The reported introductory price is about $1,200; the cost of a complete desk depends on the display and other equipment selected.

Compatibility remains the important word, but not a promise that every IBM program or expansion card will fit. The Tandy approach offers a lower-cost PCjr alternative with a familiar software target. Its November arrival makes the home-computer comparison sheet considerably more interesting.

stories.headline: A shopping mall arrives on the home-computer screen
body: Home shopping no longer requires a paper catalog in every case. Selby Bateman’s November COMPUTE! report describes CompuServe’s Electronic Mall, open around the clock, with access to more than 80 merchants. The service’s more than 130,000 subscribers provide a substantial potential audience.

WaldenBooks, American Express, Commodore, McGraw-Hill, Microsoft and American Airlines are among the named merchants. Product descriptions, shipping information, merchant mailboxes and order forms turn a terminal session into something closer to a shopping trip.

The hardware and service arrangements still vary sharply. Chicago’s Keyfax is reported at a $10–$15 monthly base rate plus a $40 software package; Viewtron requires a $600 AT&T Sceptre terminal confined to that service. American People/Link is planning nationwide service for December, not operating it yet.

stories.headline: KoalaPad gives PCjr owners a drawing surface in their laps
body: A stylus or fingertip is enough to start drawing with KoalaPad. Lee Noel’s November COMPUTE! review follows more than a month of testing the tablet and KoalaPainter on a PCjr with 128K, a disk drive, DOS 2.1 and a color display.

The roughly six-by-eight-inch pad has two buttons and a pressure-sensitive drawing area about four inches square. It plugs into a joystick port and recognizes one contact at a time. KoalaPainter supplies two drawing screens, zoom, mirror and an Oops correction feature.

The program uses 160-by-200 resolution with 16 simultaneous colors, adding halftone patterns for more apparent shades. Noel questions the choice not to use a higher-resolution mode. There is no supplied hardcopy-printing feature: pictures can be saved to disk, videotaped or photographed from the screen.

stories.headline: Copy protection must not punish the buyer
body: Mitchell Kapor takes up software piracy in November’s Creative Computing with a warning against expecting a technical cure. His comparison is retail shoplifting: control the losses, rather than assume they can be entirely eliminated.

Education, legislation, enforcement and proportionate protection all have a part in his argument. Hard-disk owners, he says, should not have to insert a specially protected floppy at the beginning of every session. Protection that obstructs the paying customer creates its own costs.

The essay discusses ADAPSO’s work on protection standards. It is a debate about policy and convenience, not a report of a particular pirate crew or arrest. As Kapor puts it, “There is no technical panacea.”

computerItems.title: Tel-A-Modem 212A
computerItems.summary: Code-A-Phone telephone with built-in modem and two phone lines for simultaneous voice and data, described in November COMPUTE!; no verified price.

computerItems.title: Archon II: Adept
computerItems.summary: November Gazette contents advertise Selby Bateman’s Inside View feature on Free Fall Associates, creators of Archon and its sequel; Order and Chaos frame the sequel. Coverage date only, not a verified launch day.

computerItems.title: Reflection
computerItems.summary: Sean Puckett’s type-in reversi game supports human-versus-human or human-versus-computer play. Originally Atari 24K; adaptations include C64, unexpanded VIC-20, TI-99/4A, Apple, IBM PC, PCjr and Color Computer.

computerItems.title: Bagdad
computerItems.summary: November Gazette publishes Bryan Files’s joystick arcade game for VIC and C64: trap genies in bottles while riding a magic carpet. Magazine availability, not commercial release.

computerItems.title: Drol and Space Change
computerItems.summary: George Miller reviews these Commodore 64 games in the November Gazette, page 107; only review presence verified.

softwareList.name: OmniWriter & OmniSpell
softwareList.detail: Human Engineered Software C64 page-oriented word processor includes a 30,000-word spelling checker. Requires disk drive and supported serial-bus or user-port parallel printer; RS-232 serial printers are unsupported. Reviewer criticizes manual page breaks.

softwareList.name: C/G Term
softwareList.detail: Robert Sims’s machine-language color/graphics terminal program appears in November Gazette, page 38, for C64 and VIC with 16K expansion. Upload/download support; disk drive and modem required. C/G BBS installment promised for next month.

softwareList.name: KoalaPainter
softwareList.detail: PCjr drawing software bundled with KoalaPad; 16 colors at 160 by 200.

priceWatch.note: $59.95 publisher price printed at end of November review, not a local sale quote.
Sharon Darling reports modem prices about $49 to $1,000 or more. $300–$500 for 1200 bps by year end is Jerry Hussong’s forecast, not a current guaranteed model price.
$600 subscriber hardware cost reported in November; service restricted to Viewtron.
Ric Manning survey, as reported by Kathy Yakal, says sysops spend on average more than $3,000 to start and another $50 monthly; these are survey averages, not product prices.

briefs.headline: 300 versus 1200 bps
briefs.summary: November modem article describes roughly 30 versus 120 characters per second. Faster transfers may reduce time-based service and long-distance bills; many local boards still operate at 300 bps.

briefs.headline: Busy signals are part of BBS life
briefs.summary: Most hobbyist boards permit only one caller at a time, unlike multi-user commercial networks; November reporting identifies 6–11 p.m. as peak use.

periodAd.headline: Writing and spelling on the Commodore 64
periodAd.summary: OmniWriter & OmniSpell combines a page-oriented word processor with a 30,000-word spelling checker. The November review lists $59.95; a disk drive and supported printer are required.

market.headline: The home-computer counter widens its pitch
market.summary: PC compatibility, graphics and sound meet in Tandy’s November newcomer; online merchants offer another way to buy software and books. Hardware choices still determine which services and accessories a household can use.

worldAnchor.headline: Discovery retrieves two stranded communications satellites
worldAnchor.summary: Discovery retrieved Palapa B2 on November 12 and Westar 6 on November 14, recovering two communications satellites stranded after booster failures. Joe Allen and Dale Gardner carried out retrieval work, with Anna Fisher operating the shuttle arm.

bbsNote.headline: BBS culture grows beyond the user-group meeting
bbsNote.summary: Kathy Yakal’s November COMPUTE! feature documents local boards, public-domain programs, online play, sysop costs and community moderation. Posts below are editorial summaries of the article, not invented historical message transcripts.

posts.text: Stan and Susie Subeck’s Atari board offers adventure games and a trivia quiz. Its menus use Valley Girl slang inspired by their daughter.

Kent Fillmore’s home Apple II board has operated for about three months; he proposes retail-linked boards with local user-group sections nationwide. The wider network is a proposal, not a completed rollout.

posts.platform: Hobbyist BBS systems surveyed by Plumb
posts.text: Reported averages exceed $3,000 startup cost, $50 monthly and up to 50 maintenance hours monthly; peak demand is 6–11 p.m.
Yakal says most boards prohibit obscene messages and copyrighted uploads; some switch to passwords or membership fees. No pirate crew is identified.

curiosity.headline: A Valley Girl BBS tells callers to “de-val”
curiosity.summary: A Chicago-area Atari bulletin board turns 1980s slang into its interface.
curiosity.detail: Stan and Susie Subeck’s Valley Girl BBS calls deleting a message “bag” and exiting “de-val.” A glossary accompanies menus inspired by their 13-year-old daughter’s speech; the board also offers online adventure games and trivia. Reported by Kathy Yakal in November COMPUTE!, not a launch assigned to this week.

gadgetWatch.headline: Sony shrinks the compact-disc player
gadgetWatch.summary: Sony’s D-50 arrives in Japan this November at ¥49,800, according to November catalog material preserved by a collector. The compact player brings CD playback to a much smaller package.
